controllingAuthority.summary: Access to the arrest cycle shall be restricted by the center for the non-conviction dispositions listed in subsection (h). Restriction is mandatory and there is no application: the clerk, the arresting agency or the prosecuting attorney reports the qualifying disposition and the center restricts. Where the restriction has not in fact been entered, the participant's route is a written request to the prosecuting attorney for the county of arrest — the Attorney General, district attorney or solicitor-general under § 35-3-37(a)(5) — who enters the restriction code in the CCH interface or forwards the approved paperwork to GCIC. GCIC then notifies the arresting agency within 30 days and the arresting agency restricts its own records within 30 days under § 35-3-37(k)(1).

exclusions: Dismissal or nolle prosse entered as part of a plea agreement that resulted in conviction on an offence arising from the same transaction (§ 35-3-37(i)).
Dismissal because the prosecuting attorney was barred from introducing material evidence (§ 35-3-37(i)).
Dismissal because the conduct was part of a pattern of criminal activity prosecuted in another jurisdiction (§ 35-3-37(i)).
Dismissal because of diplomatic or consular immunity (§ 35-3-37(i)).
Partial acquittal, where some charges resulted in acquittal and some did not (§ 35-3-37(i)).
An acquittal later shown to have resulted from jury tampering or judicial misconduct (§ 35-3-37(i)).
An acquittal within the ten days the prosecuting attorney has after the verdict to defeat restriction by clear and convincing evidence on either ground in § 35-3-37(h)(2)(E).

units.label: Automatic restriction on the qualifying disposition
units.description: Subsection (h) says access shall be restricted. There is no application and no form. The participant obtains their own Georgia criminal history, reads it for whether each charge shows a final disposition and whether the cycle is already marked restricted, and if it is, stops here and moves to the clerk-sealing and jail routes. LegalEase supplies the diagnosis, the reading guide for the report, and the confirmation step of pulling the criminal history again.

units.label: Written request to the prosecuting attorney where the restriction was not entered
units.description: Where the criminal history does not show the cycle as restricted, the participant asks the prosecuting attorney for the county of arrest to enter the restriction. LegalEase identifies the correct prosecuting office and generates the participant-signed written request setting out the arrest date, the arresting agency, the charges, the disposition and the statutory ground. Where the county prosecutor's office publishes its own intake form, that local form governs and the generated request is the covering request. LegalEase does not make the prosecutor's decision and does not enter anything in the GCIC CCH interface.

legalDesignDecision.rationale: The mechanism is mandatory and automatic, so the first unit is genuinely guidance: subsection (h) restricts on the qualifying disposition and there is no application, no petition and no statewide form. But the route does not end there. Where the restriction was never entered, GBI and georgia.gov both direct the participant to contact the prosecuting attorney for the county of arrest, and the review itself lists a request letter among the things LegalEase can prepare. A participant-signed written request to a prosecutor is packet-capable under the controlling product model, so the route is modelled as two legally distinct sequential units — an automatic mechanism with nothing to file, then a participant submission to a different actor at a different destination — rather than as a single guidance track. Correspondence rather than a court filing is not a reason to withhold a packet. Local prosecutor intake forms govern where they exist, which is why localFormOverride is set.

provenance.sourceHeading: SCOPE AND STATUS / Terminology
provenance.sourceStatement: Georgia does not use "expungement" in the statute and has not since July 1, 2013. The two remedies are **record restriction** (limiting who may see criminal history record information) and **sealing** (closing the clerk of court's file). Neither destroys the record. This is a consumer-harm-grade error and must be removed from all Georgia copy and from Wilma.

controllingAuthority.summary: An individual convicted of a misdemeanour, or of a series of misdemeanours arising from a single incident, may petition the court in which the conviction occurred to restrict access to the criminal history record information. The court shall grant the order if the individual has completed the terms of the sentence, has not been convicted of any crime in any jurisdiction excluding nonserious traffic offences for at least four years immediately preceding the filing, has no pending charged offences, and the harm to the individual clearly outweighs the public's interest in the information being publicly available. Section 35-3-37(w) applies the paragraph to sentences imposed before, on or after July 1, 2020.

exclusions: Family violence simple assault, § 16-5-20(d), unless the individual was a youthful offender under 21 at the time of arrest.
Family violence simple battery, § 16-5-23(f), unless the individual was a youthful offender.
Family violence battery, § 16-5-23.1(f), unless the individual was a youthful offender.
Family violence stalking, § 16-5-90.
Violating a family violence order, § 16-5-95.
Child molestation, § 16-6-4.
Enticing a child for indecent purposes, § 16-6-5.
Improper sexual contact by employee or agent, by a foster parent, or by a person in a position of trust, § 16-6-5.1.
Public indecency, § 16-6-8(b).
Keeping a place of prostitution, § 16-6-10.
Pimping, § 16-6-11.
Pandering by compulsion, § 16-6-12.
Sexual battery, § 16-6-22.1.
Obstructing or hindering a person making an emergency telephone call, § 16-10-24.3.
Peeping Toms, § 16-11-61.
Any offence related to minors generally under Part 2 of Article 3 of Chapter 12 of Title 16.
Theft under Chapter 8 of Title 16, except misdemeanour shoplifting or refund fraud under § 16-8-14 or § 16-8-14.1.
Any serious traffic offence under Article 15 of Chapter 6 of Title 40, which is where DUI sits.
A lifetime maximum of two convictions restricted under § 35-3-37(j)(4) has already been reached.
A petition on the same conviction denied less than two years ago, measured from the final order.

controllingAuthority.summary: Where an individual had a felony charge dismissed or nolle prossed, or was found not guilty of it, but was convicted of a misdemeanour offence that was not a lesser included offence of the felony charge, the individual may petition the court in which he or she was accused or convicted — or, if the charge was dismissed, the superior court in the county where the arrest occurred — to restrict access to criminal history record information for the felony charge, within four years of the arrest. The relief restricts the felony charge only. The court shall grant if it determines the misdemeanour conviction was not a lesser included offence of the felony charge and the harm clearly outweighs the public interest.

exclusions: A misdemeanour of conviction that was a lesser included offence of the felony charge.
A petition filed more than four years after the arrest. This is a limitations period, not a waiting period.
The misdemeanour conviction itself, which this route does not reach — only the felony charge is restricted.

waitingPeriods.duration: the petition must be filed within four years of the arrest. This is a hard deadline running from arrest, not a waiting period, and it is the opposite of every other Georgia route. An eligibility engine that treats it as a waiting period will silently produce false positives.

geography.venue: Statewide statute. The court in which the individual was accused or convicted; if the felony charge was dismissed, the superior court in the county where the arrest occurred.

destination.name: Clerk of the accusing or convicting court, or the superior court of the county of arrest where the charge was dismissed
destination.detail: Notice to the arresting law enforcement agency and the prosecuting attorney, which is broader than the other § 35-3-37(j) routes. Hearing within 90 days if requested.

components.notes: Petition to Restrict Access to Criminal History Record Information (Felony Charge), citing § 35-3-37(j)(1). No statewide judiciary form exists. Filed in the existing criminal case under the existing case number, styled State of Georgia v. Defendant, in the court that handled the case.

Proposed order directing GCIC and every agency in the county, including the arresting agency and the jail or detention centre, to restrict all criminal history record information pertaining to the case. It names the OTN and arrest date, names GCIC and the county agencies by category, names the clerk and court, and limits disclosure to what § 35-3-37(t) and (v) permit. The order restricts the felony charge only.

Certifies service on the named prosecuting attorney, identified as District Attorney or Solicitor-General, and on the Clerk of the named county court, by certified mail, e-filing or hand delivery, with the date.

The one conclusion LegalEase must not generate — that the misdemeanour of conviction was not a lesser included offence of the felony charge — is a legal conclusion the participant or their counsel asserts, and the engine routes to attorney review by default. That is a scope restriction on a packet that exists, not a reason to withhold one. The four-year period is a filing deadline running from arrest and must not share a code path with the conviction-free waiting periods on the other routes.

limitations.statement: Consumer-facing copy must say "restrict" and, separately, "seal." Georgia does not use "expungement" in the statute and has not since July 1, 2013, and neither remedy destroys the record.

provenance.sourceHeading: SCOPE AND STATUS / Terminology
provenance.sourceStatement: Georgia does not use "expungement" in the statute and has not since July 1, 2013. limitations.statement: The packet must state that a restriction or sealing may still be used to disqualify the participant from employment or office in the same manner as a first offender discharge under § 42-8-63.1, and does not supersede disclosure required by federal law. controllingAuthority.summary: Where an individual was convicted of an offence and sentenced to a punishment other than the death penalty, the conviction was vacated by the trial court or reversed by an appellate or other post-conviction court, that decision became final by the completion of the appellate process, and the prosecuting attorney has not retried the case within two years of the date the vacating or reversing order became final, the individual may petition the court in which he or she was convicted to restrict access to criminal history record information for the offence. The court weighs why the judgment was reversed or vacated, why the prosecuting attorney has not retried it, and the public interest.

exclusions: A conviction carrying a sentence of death.
A case the prosecuting attorney has retried within two years of the vacating or reversing order becoming final.
A vacating or reversing decision that has not yet become final by completion of the appellate process.

waitingPeriods.condition: Finality of the vacating or reversing order
waitingPeriods.duration: two years from the date the order became final by completion of the appellate process, during which the prosecuting attorney has not retried the case

tracks.publicName: Restricting and sealing a completed First Offender case

controllingAuthority.summary: Section 42-8-62.2, enacted by Act 403 and effective July 1, 2026, provides at (b) that at the time a defendant sentenced under the article has been exonerated and discharged without court adjudication of guilt, the court records shall be restricted. Subsection (c) provides that an individual who was exonerated of guilt and discharged, as a matter of law or pursuant to a court order, prior to July 1, 2026 may petition the court that granted such discharge for an order to seal and make unavailable to the public the criminal file, docket books, criminal minutes, final record, all other records of the court and the defendant's criminal history record information in the custody of the clerk of court, including within any index. Notice of the petition shall be sent to the clerk of court and the prosecuting attorney, and notice by registered or certified mail or statutory overnight delivery is sufficient. Under (d) the court shall order sealing within 90 days of the filing, with no findings required. The clerk seals within 60 days under (e), and under (f) the court shall also order law enforcement agencies, jails and detention centers to restrict, with compliance within 30 days.

exclusions: A First Offender sentence imposed on or after July 1, 2026, which the court restricts and seals at sentencing instead.
A case where the First Offender sentence was revoked and an adjudication of guilt entered, so that no exoneration and discharge occurred.
A participant who was never sentenced under the First Offender Act, who is on the separate retroactive first offender route under § 42-8-66.
A participant who has not yet been discharged or whose case remains operationally active, who is routed to the § 42-8-62.1(c) petition under the adopted crosswalk.

legalDesignDecision.rationale: The adopted memorandum directs custom_pleading and the signed Act confirms the mechanism. Section 42-8-62.2(c) creates a participant petition with a definite venue — the court that granted the discharge — definite notice recipients, definite contents and definite relief, and no statewide judiciary form exists, so a controlled custom pleading is the correct output. Under (d) the court shall order sealing within 90 days of the filing and the section requires no findings at all, so no balancing or privacy-harm narrative is pleaded. The statutory destination, timing, service and order treatment are preserved exactly: notice to the clerk of court and the prosecuting attorney, sufficiency of registered or certified mail or statutory overnight delivery, 90 days for the order, 60 days for the clerk under (e), and a mandatory companion order to law enforcement agencies, jails and detention centers under (f) with 30 days to comply. tracks.legalName: Petition for Retroactive First Offender Treatment, Exoneration and Discharge under O.C.G.A. § 42-8-66
tracks.publicName: Asking for First Offender treatment you should have been given

controllingAuthority.summary: An individual who qualified for first offender sentencing but was not informed of that eligibility, or who was sentenced between March 18, 1968 and October 31, 1982 to incarceration not exceeding one year and would otherwise have qualified, may petition the court in which they were convicted for retroactive first offender treatment. The petition may be filed only with the consent of the prosecuting attorney, obtained before filing. A hearing is held if requested by the petitioner or the prosecuting attorney or if the court desires one. The court may grant if it finds by a preponderance that the defendant was eligible at the time of the original sentencing, or qualifies under the 1968 to 1982 provision, and that the ends of justice and the welfare of society are served. There is no filing fee. On a grant the conviction becomes a first offender discharge, which is not a conviction, and the court sends the order to the petitioner, the prosecuting attorney, the Georgia Crime Information Center and the Department of Driver Services, both of which must modify their records.

exclusions: A participant who was in fact sentenced under the First Offender Act, who is on the § 42-8-62.1 or § 42-8-62.2 routes instead.
A sentence entered before March 18, 1968, since § 42-8-66(g) applies the Code section to any sentence entered on or after that date.
A sentence that may be modified under O.C.G.A. § 17-10-1, to which § 42-8-66(f) says this Code section does not apply.
A filing without the prosecuting attorney's advance consent. Prosecutor silence is not consent.

legalDesignDecision.rationale: Guidance is retained on a precise ground and the packet framework is recorded rather than denied. Section 42-8-66(a) permits the petition to be filed only with the prosecuting attorney's consent, obtained before filing. Securing that consent is negotiation with an opposing party, which the product model places outside self-help and which LegalEase does not do, so requires_negotiation is a preserved rationale. Packet identity is a separate question from delivery scope, and it is answered here: a legally identifiable participant petition does exist once written consent has been obtained, and its venue, contents, requested relief, hearing rule, fee rule and order distribution are recorded in the component notes. The schema has no field that stores packet capability separately from delivery scope — packetIdentity is derived from the presence of a strategy — so a composed route with an unavailable post-consent unit would be the only structural way to record it, and the adopted memorandum expressly makes such a stage conditional on counsel's later approval, which has not been given. The framework is therefore documented and the question is put to counsel rather than answered here. This route is not collapsed into a First Offender sealing route: it remains separate from the three § 42-8-62.1 and § 42-8-62.2 mechanisms and there is no old-M-to-new-L mapping.
